content: The WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Tuberculosis (TB) Diagnosis, specifically the 2021 update, provide detailed recommendations on the use of rapid diagnostic technologies for TB detection and drug resistance testing. These guidelines introduce new classes of diagnostic technologies and evaluate associated products. New Classes of Diagnostic Technologies and Evaluated Products: 1. Moderate Complexity Automated Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests (NAATs): These tests detect TB and resistance to rifampicin (RIF) and isoniazid (INH). Products evaluated include: Abbott RealTime MTB and MTB RIF/INH assays (Abbott Laboratories, USA) BD MAX MDR-TB assay (Becton Dickinson, USA) FluoroType MTBDR assay (Bruker/Hain Lifescience, Germany) Roche cobas MTB and MTB RIF/INH assays (Hoffmann-La Roche, Switzerland) 2. Low Complexity Automated NAATs: These tests detect resistance to INH and second-line anti-TB agents. Example: Xpert MTB/XDR (Cepheid, USA) 3. High Complexity Reverse Hybridization-Based NAATs: These tests detect resistance to pyrazinamide (PZA). Example: Genoscholar PZA-TB II (Nipro Corporation, Japan) 4. Biomarker-Based Lateral Flow Assay: The LF-LAM test (Alere Determine TB LAM Ag, USA) is recommended for diagnosing TB in specific groups of HIV-infected patients. A positive LF-LAM result is considered bacteriological confirmation of TB in these patients. Transition to New Diagnostic Classes: The guidelines emphasize a transitional period where previously recommended product-based diagnostics are being integrated into these new classes. Future updates aim to consolidate all products into these defined classes, ensuring consistency and clarity in recommendations. Organization of WHO-Recommended Tests: The tests are categorized based on their intended use: Initial Tests for TB Diagnosis: With drug-resistance detection Without drug-resistance detection Follow-On Diagnostic Tests: Conducted after TB confirmation. Initial Diagnostic Tests: 1. WHO-Approved Rapid Diagnostic Tests (WRDs): These tests use molecular or biomarker-based techniques for TB diagnosis. Examples of molecular WRDs include: Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and Xpert MTB/RIF (Cepheid, USA) Truenat MTB, MTB Plus, and MTB-RIF Dx tests (Molbio Diagnostics, India) TB-LAMP (Eiken Chemical, Japan) 2. Moderate Complexity Automated NAATs: These tests detect TB, RIF resistance, and INH resistance. Products include Abbott RealTime MTB, BD MAX MDR-TB, FluoroType MTBDR, and Roche cobas MTB assays. 3. LF-LAM Test: Recommended for HIV-positive patients with presumptive TB. Follow-On Diagnostic Tests: 1. Line-Probe Assays (LPAs): Detect resistance to RIF and INH (e.g., GenoType MTBDRplus, Nipro NTM+MDRTB Detection Kit). Detect resistance to fluoroquinolones (FQs) and second-line injectable agents (e.g., GenoType MTBDRsl). 2. New Classes of Follow-On Tests: Low complexity automated NAATs for detecting resistance to INH, FQs, ethionamide (ETO), and amikacin (AMK). Example: Xpert MTB/XDR. High complexity reverse hybridization NAATs for detecting PZA resistance. Example: Genoscholar PZA-TB II. Conventional Diagnostic Tests: Sputum smear microscopy remains widely used in high TB burden settings but is relatively insensitive and cannot distinguish drug-susceptible from drug-resistant strains. Culture remains the gold standard for bacteriological confirmation of TB but is not widely used as a primary diagnostic test in high-burden countries due to cost, infrastructure requirements, and long turnaround times. Xpert MTB/RIF Assay: This cartridge-based automated test uses real-time PCR to detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) and RIF resistance directly from sputum within two hours. WHO recommends its use as the initial diagnostic test for TB and RIF resistance in adults and children with pulmonary TB symptoms, TB meningitis, and extrapulmonary TB. Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra Assay: This test improves sensitivity and reliability by using two multicopy amplification targets (IS6110 and IS1081) and a larger PCR chamber, resulting in a lower limit of detection (LOD) compared to Xpert MTB/RIF. It is recommended for use in adults and children with pulmonary TB symptoms, TB meningitis, and extrapulmonary TB. Truenat MTB, MTB Plus, and MTB-RIF Dx Assays: These chip-based real-time micro PCR assays detect MTBC directly from sputum and provide results in under an hour. They are designed for use in peripheral laboratories with minimal infrastructure and training requirements. WHO recommends their use as initial diagnostic tests for TB and RIF resistance. Moderate Complexity Automated NAATs: These tests offer rapid and accurate detection of pulmonary TB and resistance to RIF and INH from respiratory samples. They are suitable for high-throughput testing in laboratory settings and require reliable systems for sample referral and result reporting. Recommendations for Implementation: WHO emphasizes the importance of transitioning from conventional microscopy to molecular WRDs for initial TB diagnosis. Culture and microscopy remain necessary for monitoring treatment response and diagnosing pediatric and extrapulmonary TB. These guidelines aim to enhance the accuracy, speed, and accessibility of TB diagnostics, ultimately improving patient outcomes and reducing transmission.
